title: A lesson for those with minds
hookLine: in their stories is a lesson for people of understanding (12:111)

cards: What are stories for? This week was a parade of people. The mighty 'Ad, told that forgiveness is strength.
Thamud and the she-camel. Ibrahim's roasted calf and Lut in his doorway. Shu'ayb and the honest scales.
Then Yusuf, the best of stories, read whole. The very last verse of Surah Yusuf answers the question, and not just for Yusuf.
It looks back over everything, the prophets of Surah Hud included, and says what a reader is supposed to do with a story once it's over.

teach.b: Verse one hundred eleven, in Pickthall's translation: "In their history verily there is a lesson for men of understanding." Two Arabic words carry it. The first is 'ibra, a lesson.
Its root, '-b-r, means to cross over, the way you cross a river; 'ubur is a crossing.
The same root gives ta'bir, the interpreting of dreams, which runs all through this surah: Yusuf crosses from the picture in the dream to what it means.
So an 'ibra is a lesson you get by crossing over, from their story to your life.
The second word is albab, minds, the plural of lubb: the core of a thing, the kernel inside the shell. Ulu al-albab, people with minds, are people who get to the core.
The verse goes on: this isn't an invented tale, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of everything, and a guidance and a mercy for people who believe.
So the Qur'an doesn't tell stories just to pass the evening, or to make you wonder how it ends. It tells them so you'll cross over.

teach.h: FROM THEIR STORY TO YOUR LIFE.
teach.b: Yusuf's brothers, jealous of a favored child: is there a jealousy in your house? The woman who lied, then confessed: is there a truth you've been holding back?
A father who said beautiful patience twice: what are you waiting through right now?
The story is told so the one hearing it can step into it, and come out somewhere else.

how: Muslim teachers close a study of Surah Yusuf with 12:111 and ask students to draw lessons, 'ibar, from the story for their own lives; the phrase ulu al-albab recurs throughout the Qur'an for people of reflection.

o: a lesson you cross over into, from their story to yours
a warning of punishment for those who don't listen
a written rule taken word for word from a story

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: a crossing, as of a river

s: 'ibra shares a root with crossing a river
'-b-r: to cross over. a lesson is crossing from their story to your life.
it says 'in their stories', looking back over the prophets' stories.
the root of 'ibra also gives the word for interpreting dreams
ta'bir: Yusuf crosses from the dream to its meaning.

games.q: you've finished Surah Yusuf. according to its last verse, what is the story for?
o: to show how clever Yusuf was.
a lesson for those with minds.
games.why: a lesson for people of understanding: no invented tale, but guidance and a mercy for those who believe.

practice: Let the story pass in front of you: the dream, the well, the house, the prison, the palace, the brothers bowing. Where does it touch your life?
Let one lesson come, in a single plain sentence of your own; if you pray, ask to understand it.

wordCard.voice: 'Ibra. A lesson you cross over into, from their story to your life, the word that closes Surah Yusuf. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "a lesson for those with minds" (12:111): 'ibra, a crossing lesson; albab, the cores.

carryVoice: Your line: the story is the lesson. Their story, crossed over into yours. Day four hundred forty-one, and a week complete.
